what-is-strike.title: What is Strike? A plain-English guide to the exchange
what-is-strike.subtitle: What you can trade on Strike, how copy trading works, who it is for, and how a first visit goes, in plain words for people who have never traded a perp.

faq.q: Do I need ADA or a Cardano wallet?
faq.a: No. An Ethereum or Solana wallet works too, and deposits can be made by card.
No. Stocks, indices and commodities trade on the same account as Bitcoin, as perps.

faq.q: Can I copy a trader instead of trading myself?
faq.a: Yes. Copy trading places a trade on your account whenever the trader you chose makes one, within limits you set.

what-is-strike.html:
What is Strike?

Strike Finance is a perpetual futures exchange. A perpetual future, or perp, is a contract that follows the price of something, such as Bitcoin or Tesla, without you owning it. You can profit if the price rises, by going long, or if it falls, by going short.

Strike started on Cardano in May 2025. It now runs its own trading engine with an order book, the system large exchanges use. Buyers and sellers post the prices they want, and the engine matches them. Your funds sit in smart contracts on the blockchain, and your balance is held in US dollars.

What can you trade?

Strike lists 34 markets. They fall into four groups.

TypeExamples
CryptoBitcoin, Ethereum, Solana, XRP, Cardano, HYPE
StocksNvidia, Tesla, Alphabet, Coinbase, Micron, SpaceX
IndicesS&P 500, Nasdaq-100
CommoditiesGold, silver, WTI crude oil

Everything sits on one account and one balance. You do not need a separate stock broker to trade Nvidia next to Bitcoin.

What is copy trading?

Copy trading lets Strike place trades on your account whenever a trader you choose makes a trade. You can copy traders on Strike, or any wallet on Hyperliquid, a large exchange where every trade is public. You choose how big each copied trade is, and you can cap how much of your balance it uses.

Who it's for

  • You trade crypto and want stocks or gold too. A Bitcoin trade and a gold trade can sit on the same account.
  • You would rather not pick every trade. You copy a trader whose record you have checked, with limits so one bad run cannot take your whole balance.
  • You are new to trading. Connect a wallet, deposit a small amount, and learn while the numbers are small. This series walks you through it.

How to get started

  1. Go to app.strikefinance.org in a browser, or use the Strike mobile app.
  2. Sign in by connecting a wallet. Wallets on Cardano, Ethereum and Solana all work.
  3. Deposit. Send crypto from a Cardano, Ethereum, Solana, Base, Arbitrum or Bitcoin wallet, or pay by card up to $50,000. Coins that move in price are swapped to dollars on arrival, so your balance is always in US dollars.
  4. Look around before you trade. The Trade page shows the chart and the order panel; Copy Trading and Earn have their own menus.

A worked example

This is an example, not a suggestion. Say you deposit $100 and open a $100 long on gold with no leverage. If gold rises 5%, your position is worth about $105, less a small trading fee. If gold falls 5%, it is worth about $95.

With leverage, both of those moves get bigger. That is the topic of guide 3.

Things worth knowing

  • Leverage can liquidate you. If a leveraged trade moves far enough against you, the exchange closes it and you lose the money behind it. Guide 4 explains how to keep clear of that.
  • Withdrawals have limits. Strike caps how much can leave in any rolling 1-hour and 24-hour window. If a withdrawal would go over the cap, it waits until earlier withdrawals age out of the window.
  • Copying a trader does not copy their results. Your copy uses your own leverage and size, and it starts from the moment you subscribe. Your results can differ from theirs.

How I use it

How I use it

I do not trade by hand. I copy two traders from Hyperliquid on Strike, one on my main account and one on a sub-account. I check every trader's full history first. My rule: decide your limits before your first copy, not after your first loss.

what-is-a-perp.title: What is a perp? Perpetual futures explained in plain English
what-is-a-perp.subtitle: A perpetual future follows a price and never expires. What that means, how hourly funding keeps it close to the real price, and how to find a market on Strike.

faq.q: Do I own any Bitcoin when I buy a BTC perp?
faq.a: No. You hold a contract that follows Bitcoin's price, backed by the dollars in your Strike account.
It does not. A perp runs until you close it or it is closed for you, which is what the liquidation guide explains.

faq.q: Can I profit when prices fall?
faq.a: Yes. Going short on a perp earns when the price drops, and loses when it rises.

faq.q: Why is the perp's price slightly different from the real price?
faq.a: The perp trades on its own order book, so it drifts. Hourly funding pulls it back towards the index price.

toc.title: How to find a market on Strike

what-is-a-perp.html:
What is a perp?

A future is an agreement to trade something at a set price on a set date. A perpetual future, or perp, drops the date. The contract keeps running for as long as you hold it, and its price follows the asset it is named after.

On Strike, a BTC-USD perp follows the price of Bitcoin. If you think the price will rise, you go long: you profit as it climbs. If you think it will fall, you go short: you profit as it drops.

Either way you never hold any Bitcoin. Your position is a number on the exchange, backed by the dollars in your account.

What keeps the price honest?

Nothing forces a perp to match the asset on its own, so exchanges use funding. The exchange compares the perp's price with an index price, a reference built from the asset's price on other venues. When the perp trades above the index, longs pay shorts a small fee; when it trades below, shorts pay longs. On Strike, funding is settled every hour, on the hour.

The payments are tiny per hour. In Strike's own example, the rate is 0.00125% an hour. On a $100 position that is about a tenth of a cent, paid or received, every hour.

TermMeaning
LongYou profit when the price rises
ShortYou profit when the price falls
Index priceThe asset's price elsewhere, used as the reference
Mark priceThe price Strike uses to value your position
FundingHourly payment between longs and shorts

Who it's for

  • You want to trade a move, not hold the asset. No wallet for the coin, no broker for the share, no vault for the gold.
  • You want to be able to go short. A spot purchase only profits when prices rise. A perp lets you take the other side.
  • You want one account for different things. On Strike the same balance trades crypto, stocks, indices and commodities.

How to find a market on Strike

  1. Open app.strikefinance.org and sign in with your wallet.
  2. Click the market name at the top left of the Trade page, BTC-USD by default. A list opens.
  3. Use the tabs to narrow it: Crypto, TradFi for stocks, indices and commodities, and a search box for a name.
  4. Each row shows the last price, the 24-hour change, the volume and the current funding rate. Pick one and the chart and order panel switch to it.

A worked example

This is an example, not a suggestion. Say you open a $100 long on the BTC-USD perp with no leverage, and Bitcoin rises 5%. Your position is now worth about $105. Close it and you keep the $5, less a small trading fee on the way in and out.

If Bitcoin had fallen 5% instead, closing would leave you about $95.

A short works in reverse. Open a $100 short, and a 5% fall earns about $5 while a 5% rise loses about $5. Funding adds or takes a fraction of a cent an hour while the position is open.

Things worth knowing

  • Funding runs both ways. Depending on the market, you may pay or receive it. The rate shows next to each market in the list.
  • Fees are small but real. Strike's base fee for taking liquidity is 0.050% of the trade's value, and placing a resting order earns a 0.005% rebate.
  • Leverage changes everything. The examples above use none. With leverage a smaller move produces the same gain or loss, and a large enough move closes the trade. That is the next two guides.
